sections.title: Start here: what a buyer of a storage platform is actually paying for
ps: Brookfield agreed in July 2026 to pay about USD 7 billion of {{enterprise value}} for Aypa — a company that publishes no revenue, no project list and no leadership page. This guide teaches what that money buys: a book of long-term contracts, a pipeline of {{queue position}}s and land, a financing machine that turns permits into operating batteries, and about 200 people who run it. It then teaches how the machine converts a pipeline into operating capacity, how it is financed layer by layer, how the credits are monetised, how a {{financial sponsor}} gets out, and where the whole structure fails.

**What it deliberately does not repeat:** how a battery earns money hour by hour — the {{tolling agreement}} revenue model, {{ancillary services}} stacking and the duration-and-degradation arithmetic are taught in the Classroom and in the storage-owner material this corpus already holds. Here the battery is an asset on a balance sheet, and the question is what it is worth to the next owner.

**One idea carries the guide.** A platform is worth the risks it has already retired. Every rung a project climbs — site, queue, permit, contract, financing, construction, operation — removes one thing that could go wrong, and a buyer pays for the rungs, not the megawatts.

sections.title: Four things inside the price
ps: Take the buyer's own words apart. Brookfield said it would acquire 'Aypa's operating, under-construction and contracted project portfolio, together with its development platform and approximately 200-person team'. That is three of the four things, and the fourth — the bank relationships — is implied by a company that has closed nine financings with the same fifteen lenders.

**The contracted book.** About 6.5 GW 'operating, under-construction and contracted', '95% contracted under long-term agreements with investment-grade customers for an average remaining contract life of 17 years'. Two numbers matter here more than the gigawatts: {{percent contracted}} tells a lender how much of the cash flow is fixed, and {{average remaining contract life}} tells it for how long. A portfolio that is 95 per cent contracted for 17 years can carry a great deal of debt; the same megawatts sold {{merchant}} could carry a fraction.

**The pipeline.** '>20 GW development pipeline' — projects at every earlier rung, from a land option to a permitted site waiting for a contract. A pipeline is mostly options: the right to keep spending on a project if the next study or hearing goes well. Its value is the sum of many small probabilities, and it is where a buyer's and seller's models disagree most.

**The team and the machine.** In-house development, transmission analytics, procurement, construction and operations, per Aypa's own regulatory testimony. A buyer of a {{platform sale}} is paying for the ability to make more projects, not for a fixed set of them — which is why the 200 people are in the sentence.

**The subtraction.** {{enterprise value}} minus equity value is debt. USD 7 billion minus USD 3 billion leaves about USD 4 billion of project and holding-company borrowing that stays with the assets and passes to the new owner. The seller's cheque is the equity value; the buyer's true cost is the enterprise value.

sections.title: Who holds the dispatch rights: reading a storage contract from the outside
ps: Aypa's contracts come in five forms, and the difference between them is who decides when the battery charges and discharges — the {{dispatch rights}}. Hold those and you hold the revenue risk; give them away and you are paid a fee.

**A utility toll (SDG&E at Cald, SRP at Pediment).** The utility pays a fixed monthly amount per megawatt for twenty years and dispatches the battery itself. Aypa's income is the fee; its risk is availability — being there when called. This is the form a lender likes best, and it is why Brookfield could say 'investment-grade customers'.

**An {{energy storage service agreement}} (NCPA at Trolley).** The same idea, bought by a joint-action agency on behalf of eight municipal utilities. Public power buys capacity the way it buys a transmission line: for reliability, on a long term, from a private owner who builds and maintains it.

**Resource adequacy with energy settlement (PG&E at Marici, Gabriel and Dirac).** California's version: the utility buys the battery's contribution to its reserve requirement, approved by the commission, with an energy settlement layered on. The contract date and the interconnection date can diverge — PG&E's evaluator flagged queue dates of 2031 and 2033 against 2027 deliveries.

**Build-own-operate with the utility holding dispatch (Santee Cooper at Pinopolis).** The public utility leases the land, keeps 'exclusive dispatch control', and Aypa constructs, owns and operates — a toll in all but name, on a retired coal site that earns the {{energy community bonus}}.

**Hybrid PPA with a community-choice aggregator (San Diego Community Power at Vidal).** Energy, resource adequacy and renewable certificates from a solar-plus-storage site, bought by the entity that serves retail customers in place of the utility. A {{solar-plus-storage}} project sells three products through one contract.

What none of these forms does is leave Aypa exposed to the hourly price. The two ERCOT batteries financed without a named counterparty (Wolf Tank, Borden County) are the exception, and the buyer's '95% contracted' is the measure of how small that exception is.

sections.title: Two ways to sell a tax credit
ps: A battery earns an investment tax credit that a developer with little taxable income cannot use. Aypa's record shows both ways of turning that credit into construction money, sometimes in the same year.

**The {{partnership flip}}.** A bank becomes a partner in the project company and takes most of the tax benefits until it has earned its target return, after which its share flips down and the developer keeps the cash. U.S. Bancorp Impact Finance did this at Cald–Borden County and Kuna; Morgan Stanley Renewables did it at Bypass in a 'hybrid' form that mixes a flip with a transfer. The investor's money arrives at COD, so a bridge loan carries the project until then.

**The transfer.** Since {{tax credit transferability}} arrived in 2023, the credit can simply be sold to a corporate buyer for cash. Pediment's financing used a 'tax credit transfer bridge loan' — a lender advancing the sale proceeds. Aypa has never named a buyer; nor has any private developer in this corpus.

Why both? A flip brings depreciation as well as the credit and a partner who has done the diligence; a transfer is simpler and faster but sells only the credit. The choice is a pricing decision made project by project, and the FEOC rules that now govern which batteries qualify make it a supply-chain decision too — Aypa's only named battery vendor is Canadian Solar's e-STORAGE.

sections.title: How a sponsor exits: the sale of a platform, step by step
ps: **The decision.** A {{financial sponsor}} holds a company for a period, not forever. Blackstone bought NRStor C&I in March 2020 with about 200 MWh of projects; by 2026 the platform had 6.5 GW contracted and a USD 1.55 billion corporate facility, and Infralogic reported teasers for 'Project Alpha' going out in February 2026 with Bank of America and Cantor Fitzgerald advising.

**The buyer.** A {{platform sale}} of contracted infrastructure attracts a different buyer from a single project: a fund that wants a machine and a book of long-dated cash flows. Brookfield bought through 'the second vintage of its global transition strategy' with its listed renewable affiliate co-investing — about USD 420 million or 760 million net to that affiliate, depending on which Brookfield document you read.

**The price.** Quoted two ways: about USD 7 billion of {{enterprise value}} 'at closing' and USD 3 billion of equity value. The buyer's own capacity numbers let an analyst divide: Enerdatics gets about USD 1.1 million per MW, 'just below the ~$1.27mn/MW median for comparable US standalone battery assets'. The seller's {{MOIC}} — Enerdatics' 6.2x — cannot be checked because the entry price was never disclosed.

**The gap between signing and closing.** 'Subject to customary regulatory approvals.' Between the two dates the seller still owns the company, the company's site still says 'A Blackstone Portfolio Company', and every lender with a change-of-control clause is deciding whether the new sponsor's credit is as good as the old one's. Aypa's July 2026 sale had not closed by September; the corporate facility and the warehouse are the two instruments to watch.
**What the buyer does next.** Refinance or keep the facilities, decide which pipeline options to keep funding, and put its own name on the site. None of that is public yet.

sections.title: Contracted platform or merchant platform: the view from the buyer's chair
sections.intro: The same battery can be sold on a 20-year toll or into the hourly market. A platform buyer prices the two very differently. The cards read the trade from an infrastructure fund's seat; the merchant case is this corpus's Spearmint guide.

sections.title: Where it fails
ps: **The county says no.** Kingfisher Reserve (200 MW / 800 MWh) was denied unanimously by a county board after a two-hour hearing; Dirac was refused by a city planning commission six months after the state commission had approved its contract. A {{conditional use permit}} is the rung that money cannot buy, and it is where a multi-gigawatt pipeline loses projects one hearing at a time.

**The queue is slower than the contract.** PG&E's own evaluator flagged interconnection dates of 2031 and 2033 against contracted deliveries in 2027. A contract that starts before the grid connection exists is a promise the developer may have to pay to keep.

**The numbers drift.** Aypa's own project count went from 30 to 42 in two months; the buyer said 35. A pipeline of options is easy to count generously, and a buyer's diligence is largely the work of counting it strictly.

**The supply chain is one vendor.** Canadian Solar's e-STORAGE is the only battery supplier any Aypa-side source names, with Sungrow units at one site. Under FEOC rules the credit that the {{partnership flip}} and the transfer both depend on can be lost by the wrong cell.

**The debt was priced on the old sponsor.** Every facility in the stack was signed while Blackstone owned the platform. A change of control lets lenders reprice or exit; the buyer's first job is to find out which will.
**The deal does not close.** 'Subject to customary regulatory approvals' is a condition, not a formality. Until closing, the seller carries the company and the market watches the calendar.

cards.q: A platform is sold at USD 7 billion enterprise value and USD 3 billion equity value. What does the buyer take on besides the equity cheque?
cards.a: About USD 4 billion of debt that stays with the assets — project loans, the warehouse and the corporate facility — which is why enterprise value, not equity value, is the buyer's cost.

cards.q: Name the two numbers that tell a lender how much debt a contracted storage portfolio can carry.
cards.a: Percent contracted (how much of the cash flow is fixed) and average remaining contract life (for how long).

cards.q: What does a queue position retire, and how is it usually paid for?
cards.a: The risk of never connecting to the grid; it is held with interconnection deposits, usually posted as letters of credit from a corporate LC facility.

cards.q: What is a warehouse facility for?
cards.a: Funding several projects through construction at once from one revolving loan, each project leaving the warehouse when it is refinanced at commercial operation.

cards.q: Under a utility toll, who holds the dispatch rights and what risk does the owner keep?
cards.a: The utility dispatches; the owner keeps availability risk — being there when called — and earns a fixed fee.

cards.q: Contrast a partnership flip with a credit transfer.
cards.a: A flip makes a tax investor a partner that takes tax benefits (credit and depreciation) until a target return, then flips down; a transfer sells the credit alone to a corporate buyer for cash. Both usually need a bridge loan until COD.

cards.q: Why does a resource-adequacy contract dated 2027 with a queue date of 2031 matter?
cards.a: The developer has promised delivery before the grid connection exists; the gap is a risk it may have to pay to close, and the utility's evaluator flagged exactly that.

cards.q: What happens to a platform's loans when the sponsor sells it?
cards.a: Change-of-control clauses let lenders reprice or exit; the buyer must find out which facilities survive the new sponsor.

cards.q: Why does a buyer count a pipeline strictly when the seller counts it generously?
cards.a: A pipeline is options at many stages; the seller counts every option, the buyer prices each by its probability of climbing the next rung.

cards.q: What is the one rung on the development ladder that money cannot buy?
cards.a: The local permit — a conditional use permit or rezoning decided at a public hearing, which is where Aypa lost Kingfisher Reserve and Dirac.

items.q: A seller says its platform has '6.5 GW operating, under construction and contracted'. What is the first split a buyer asks for?
c: Operating versus under construction versus contracted-but-unbuilt
items.why: Each category sits on a different rung with different risk; the buyer's own release split it 3,000 MW operating and under construction against 3,500 MW contracted.

items.q: Which instrument advances the money a tax-equity investor will pay at COD so construction can start?
items.why: The bridge loan is repaid the day the tax-equity or credit-transfer proceeds arrive at commercial operation.

items.q: A public power agency signs a 20-year energy storage service agreement and dispatches the battery itself. What is the owner's main risk?
items.why: The buyer holds dispatch rights and price risk; the owner is paid a fee for being available.

items.q: Enterprise value USD 7 billion, equity value USD 3 billion. Roughly how much debt passes to the buyer?
c: None — debt is repaid at closing
items.why: Enterprise value minus equity value is net debt; the projects' loans stay with the assets.

items.q: Why might a buyer value a pipeline of 20 GW at a small fraction of an operating gigawatt?
c: Most pipeline projects are options that may never climb the next rung
items.why: Value rises with each retired risk; early-stage projects have retired few.

items.q: Which is a sign that a platform's binding constraint has moved from capital to permitting?
c: A larger corporate facility each year alongside county denials
items.why: Aypa expanded its facilities three years running while losing two local permits — money was not the bottleneck.

items.q: What does 'subject to customary regulatory approvals' mean for who owns the company today?
c: The buyer owns it from signing
The seller owns it until closing
items.why: Signing creates an obligation to close; ownership transfers at closing, which had not happened by September 2026.

items.q: A developer's only named battery supplier is one Chinese-headquartered integrator. Which financing layer is most directly exposed to FEOC rules?
items.why: FEOC rules decide whether the project's credit can be claimed at all, which is what tax equity and transfers are buying.
